Power of Attorney Abuse in Texas (2026 Guide): Warning Signs Families Should Not Ignore

Giving someone power of attorney is a major decision.

You’re placing enormous trust in another person and allowing them to:

  • Handle finances
  • Access accounts
  • Manage property
  • Make important legal or medical decisions

In many families, this works exactly as intended.

But unfortunately, sometimes it doesn’t.

And when abuse happens, families are often left wondering:

👉 “Was this legal… or was someone taking advantage of them?”

Power of attorney abuse is a serious issue in Texas, especially involving:

  • Elderly parents
  • Incapacitated adults
  • Family conflicts
  • Financial exploitation

Let’s break down what power of attorney abuse looks like, warning signs to watch for, and what families can do if they suspect something is wrong.

What Is a Power of Attorney?

A power of attorney (POA) is a legal document that allows one person (the “agent”) to act on behalf of another person (the “principal”).

Depending on the type of POA, the agent may have authority to:

  • Access bank accounts
  • Pay bills
  • Handle investments
  • Sell property
  • Sign legal documents
  • Make healthcare decisions

This authority can be extremely broad.

And that’s exactly why abuse can become so dangerous.

What Is Power of Attorney Abuse?

Power of attorney abuse occurs when the agent:
👉 Uses their authority for improper personal benefit instead of acting in the principal’s best interests.

In Texas, agents under a POA have:
👉 Fiduciary duties

That means they must:

  • Act honestly
  • Act loyally
  • Avoid self-dealing
  • Follow the principal’s wishes when possible

When they violate those duties, legal problems can arise quickly.

Common Examples of POA Abuse

Unfortunately, abuse can take many forms.

1. Stealing Money From Accounts

This is one of the most common situations.

Examples include:

  • Unauthorized withdrawals
  • Transferring funds to themselves
  • Draining savings accounts
  • Using the principal’s money for personal expenses

2. Changing Ownership of Property

An abusive agent may attempt to:

  • Transfer property into their own name
  • Add themselves to deeds
  • Sell assets improperly

3. Isolating the Principal From Family

Sometimes abuse is accompanied by:

  • Restricted communication
  • Blocking access to family members
  • Controlling information

This can make it harder for others to detect financial exploitation.

4. Excessive “Gifts”

An agent may suddenly begin:

  • Writing large checks to themselves
  • Claiming the principal “wanted them to have it”
  • Making unusual transfers inconsistent with prior behavior

5. Manipulating an Elderly or Vulnerable Person

Power imbalances become especially concerning when:

  • Dementia
  • Cognitive decline
  • Illness
  • Dependency

are involved.

Warning Signs Families Should Watch For

Potential red flags include:

  • Missing money or unexplained transactions
  • Sudden changes in finances
  • Unpaid bills despite available funds
  • Secretive behavior by the agent
  • New “loans” or gifts
  • Sudden property transfers
  • Changes in estate plans late in life
  • Isolation of the vulnerable individual

One issue alone may not prove abuse.

But patterns matter.

Can an Agent Legally Gift Themselves Money?

Sometimes—but only in limited situations.

The authority to make gifts usually must be:
👉 Clearly authorized in the POA document

Even then:

  • The agent still must act in the principal’s best interests
  • Excessive or suspicious transfers may still be challenged

Does a Power of Attorney Continue After Death?

No.

This is one of the most misunderstood parts of POA law.

👉 A power of attorney ends immediately upon death.

After death:

  • Executors
  • Trustees
  • Probate courts

take over authority regarding the estate.

Any attempt to use a POA after death can create serious legal issues.

What Can Families Do If They Suspect Abuse?

If something feels wrong, it’s important to act carefully and quickly.

1. Gather Financial Information

Look for:

  • Bank statements
  • Property transfers
  • Account activity
  • Missing assets
  • Unusual transactions

Documentation is critical.

2. Review the POA Document

The actual authority granted matters.

Some POAs:

  • Are broad
  • Are limited
  • Restrict gifting authority
  • Limit financial transactions

3. Speak With an Attorney

An attorney can help evaluate:

  • Whether fiduciary duties were violated
  • Whether financial exploitation occurred
  • What legal remedies may be available

4. Consider Court Action if Necessary

In serious cases, courts may:

  • Revoke the POA
  • Order accountings
  • Reverse transactions
  • Remove the agent
  • Award damages

Can Criminal Charges Apply?

Potentially, yes.

Serious financial exploitation involving vulnerable adults can sometimes lead to:

  • Fraud investigations
  • Elder exploitation claims
  • Criminal theft allegations

The outcome depends on the facts and evidence involved.

Why These Cases Become So Emotional

POA abuse cases often involve:

  • Parents and children
  • Siblings
  • Long-standing family tensions
  • Inheritance disputes

And many times:
👉 The accused agent is a trusted family member.

That’s what makes these situations so difficult emotionally.

Common Misunderstandings About POA Abuse

“The Agent Can Do Whatever They Want.”

Incorrect.

Agents still owe fiduciary duties.

“If the Parent Signed the POA, Nothing Can Be Challenged.”

Also incorrect.

Abuse and exploitation claims may still exist.

“It’s Only Abuse if Money Was Stolen.”

Not necessarily.

Mismanagement, self-dealing, and coercion can also create legal problems.

“Family Members Automatically Have Access to Financial Information.”

Not always.

Authority depends on legal status and documentation.

How The Lange Firm Helps Texas Families Handle POA Disputes

At The Lange Firm, we help Texas families navigate complex situations involving:

  • Power of attorney abuse
  • Financial exploitation
  • Elder law concerns
  • Fiduciary disputes
  • Probate and estate litigation

Because when financial control and vulnerable family members are involved, small issues can escalate quickly into major legal conflicts.

Final Takeaway

Power of attorney documents are designed to protect people—not give someone unlimited control.

In Texas:
👉 Agents under a POA have serious legal responsibilities.

When someone abuses that authority through:

  • Financial exploitation
  • Self-dealing
  • Improper transfers
  • Manipulation

families may have legal options available.

Recognizing the warning signs early can make a major difference in protecting vulnerable loved ones and preserving estate assets.
